polities.name: Kingdom of France
polities.description: Valois France exits the Hundred Years’ War as a bruised but consolidating territorial monarchy. Charles VII and Louis XI claw back English continental footholds and clip Burgundian and feudal autonomy; Brittany is absorbed through dynastic marriage. Sixteenth-century Valois kings fight Habsburgs in Italy and along the Rhine, then tear the realm in the Wars of Religion. Henri IV’s Bourbon settlement (Nantes, 1598) closes the century with a reunited Catholic crown tolerating a Huguenot minority. Royal fiscal-military growth, parlements, and a Paris-centered court culture remake the medieval patchwork into an early modern state—still short of Louis XIV’s later frontiers.
polities.conflicts: Hundred Years’ War vs England (to Castillon 1453); Armagnac–Burgundian feud and League of the Public Weal; Burgundian collapse wars; Italian Wars vs Habsburgs (1494–1559) including Pavia (1525); Habsburg encirclement under Charles V/Philip II; French Wars of Religion (1562–1598) with St Bartholomew and the Catholic League; interventions in Scotland and against Spain.
polities.leaders: Charles VI; Charles VII; Joan of Arc (captain of the sacred campaign); Louis XI; Charles VIII; Louis XII; Francis I; Henry II; Catherine de’ Medici; Charles IX; Henry III; Henry IV of Navarre/Bourbon.
polities.religion: Catholic monarchy with Gallican royal claims over the French church. Huguenot (Calvinist) minority grows mid-century among nobles and towns; politiques seek peace over purity. Edict of Nantes (1598) grants limited coexistence after decades of confessional civil war—an uneasy truce, not full toleration.
polities.culture: Late Gothic yields to French Renaissance courts at Fontainebleau; vernacular chronicle and poetry (Marot, Ronsard’s Pléiade), printing, and absolutist ceremonial rise. Occitan south remains culturally distinct under northern political victory; châteaux of the Loire stage a new royal lifestyle.
polities.summary: Valois France exits the Hundred Years’ War as a bruised but consolidating territorial monarchy. Charles VII and Louis XI claw back English footholds, break Burgundian autonomy, and absorb Brittany by marriage. Sixteenth-century kings fight…
polities.story: Joan of Arc’s relief of Orléans (1429) and the Reims crowning of Charles VII turned a dynastic civil-and-foreign war into a sacred rescue narrative—then her English burning and later rehabilitation fixed her as France’s martyr-saint of sovereignty. Louis XI’s spider-king craft undone Charles the Bold at Nancy’s aftermath; Charles VIII’s 1494 descent into Naples opened the Italian Wars that would bleed Valois prestige for sixty years. St Bartholomew’s Day (1572)—a royal wedding turned confessional massacre—scarred Europe; Henri of Navarre’s ‘Paris is worth a mass’ pragmatism and Nantes ended the nightmare.
polities.literature: Froissart’s afterlife; Commynes’ memoirs of Louis XI; Rabelais’s carnivalesque giants; Ronsard and the Pléiade remaking French lyric; Montaigne’s Essais inventing the self-examining modern essay amid civil war.

polities.name: Kingdom of England
polities.description: Lancastrian England opens the century still claiming the French crown and holding Gascony; defeat in France (1453) coincides with the Wars of the Roses. Tudor consolidation under Henry VII/VIII recenters power on a stronger English monarchy, break with Rome, and naval-commercial ambition. Elizabethan England survives Spanish Armada pressure, expands Atlantic venturing, and tightens hold on Ireland. Calais—the last continental bridgehead—falls to France in 1558. Map focus is the island kingdom plus fleeting French footholds, not later British Isles unions.
polities.conflicts: Hundred Years’ War finale; Wars of the Roses; Anglo-Scottish wars (Flodden side); Tudor reconquest and plantation pressures in Ireland; war with Spain (Armada 1588); continental interventions in the Dutch Revolt and French Wars of Religion; Pilgrimage of Grace and other Tudor rebellions.
polities.leaders: Henry IV; Henry V; Henry VI; Edward IV; Richard III; Henry VII; Henry VIII; Edward VI; Mary I; Elizabeth I; ministers Wolsey, Cromwell, Cecil, Walsingham.
polities.religion: Late medieval Catholicism with Lollard undercurrents yields to Henrician schism, Edwardian Protestantism, Marian restoration, and Elizabethan settlement—a via media enforced by Uniformity, with Puritan pressure and Catholic recusancy as permanent tensions. Vernacular Bible and Book of Common Prayer reshape literacy and identity.
polities.culture: Chaucerian afterlife into print; Tudor court humanism; grammar schools; theatre as urban business; wool-and-cloth commercial society hardening into Atlantic ambition.

Meanwhile Shakespeare’s London stages kings and commoners for a ticket-buying public, and the Book of Common Prayer teaches a realm to pray in English.

polities.name: Kingdom of Scotland
polities.description: Stewart Scotland remains an independent kingdom allied by Auld Alliance to France against England. James IV’s disaster at Flodden (1513) and later Reformation turmoil under Mary Queen of Scots reshape the realm. By 1560 Scotland adopts a Calvinist kirk; in 1603 James VI inherits England (personal union), but the kingdoms stay legally separate through 1600’s map year.

polities.name: Nasrid Emirate of Granada
polities.description: Last Muslim polity on the Iberian Peninsula, paying parias and playing Castile against itself from the Alhambra. polities.description: Elective empire of princes, free cities, and ecclesiastical states—not a centralized kingdom. Luxemburg then Habsburg emperors (from Frederick III/Maximilian I/Charles V) try to weld authority while the Reformation fractures confessional unity (Peace of Augsburg 1555). Italian imperial claims fade under French and Spanish wars; Swiss de facto exit. Map shows the German-Central European imperial envelope; major members (Bohemia, Habsburg Austria) are also listed separately.

polities.leaders: Sigismund; Frederick III; Maximilian I; Charles V; Ferdinand I; Maximilian II; Rudolf II; electors of Saxony, Palatinate, Brandenburg, Mainz, Trier, Cologne, Bohemia.

polities.culture: Imperial diets; university humanism (Erfurt, Wittenberg, Tübingen); print revolution; polycentric urban culture from Nuremberg to Cologne; Meistersinger and civic pride.

polities.name: Golden Horde (late / Great Horde)
polities.description: Fragmenting Jochid successor still claiming suzerainty over Rus’ princes into the 15th century. Great Stand on the Ugra (1480) symbolizes Muscovy’s emancipation; the Great Horde collapses under Crimean and Muscovite blows by the early 1500s—clearing space for Crimean, Kazan, and Astrakhan successor politics.

polities.religion: Islamized Jochid elite; shamanic residues among steppe populations; fiscal relations with Christian Rus’ as political theology of domination fading.
polities.culture: Steppe imperial remnants; tribute politics; Turko-Mongol aristocratic tradition; caravan and raid economies.
